summary: Defines the architectural framework for Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES), where the parts of a network device that forward packets are separated from the parts that control them. It identifies the entities involved and how they interact. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: ForCES describes how a network device can separate the parts that make control decisions from the parts that forward packets. It names their roles and explains how they can associate and communicate.

questions: separating control and forwarding in routers
what is the difference between a control element and a forwarding element
what is the fp reference point in forces
subtitle: A framework for separating a network device’s control and packet-forwarding functions.

tldr.problem: Network devices often combine control decisions and packet forwarding through proprietary interfaces, limiting the ability to combine components.
tldr.mechanism: ForCES names control elements, forwarding elements, managers, and their reference points, and defines the Fp interface as the target for a separate protocol specification.
tldr.outcome: The RFC provides an architectural framework, not the ForCES protocol itself. It focuses first on control and forwarding elements that are physically close.

today: RFC 3746 is an Informational framework published in April 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the RFC leaves the ForCES Protocol to a separate specification.

sections.title: Why Separate Control and Forwarding
sections.content:
A network element such as a router can contain control elements (CEs) and forwarding elements (FEs). CEs run control and signaling protocols. FEs use hardware to process packets as directed by CEs.

ForCES provides a framework for standardizing information exchange between these parts. The RFC describes how standard interfaces could let components from different suppliers work together and let a device add control or forwarding capacity without replacing the entire system.
sections.plainLanguage: The control element decides how traffic should be handled, and the forwarding element applies those decisions to packets. ForCES describes a shared way for these separate parts to communicate.

sections.title: Elements and Reference Points
sections.content:
A ForCES network element may contain one or more CEs and one or more FEs. The CE-to-FE interaction is called Fp. Other named reference points cover CE-to-CE, FE-to-FE, manager-to-element, and manager-to-manager interactions. These reference points describe architecture; the ForCES Protocol is defined only for Fp.

CE and FE managers help decide which elements belong together before an association exists. FEs perform packet work as directed by CEs and do not coordinate their own redundancy or load sharing. The CEs coordinate those arrangements while the complete network element continues to appear as one device externally.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework names each kind of connection so it is clear which parts are communicating. Only the connection between a control element and a forwarding element is in the protocol’s scope.

sections.title: Association and Ongoing Communication
sections.content:
Before association, the CE and FE managers determine which elements should work together and provide configuration. This phase is outside the ForCES Protocol. After the elements know their roles, they communicate over Fp.

Association establishment includes a security exchange, a request to join, a query about FE capabilities, a description of the FE using its model, and optional initial configuration. Packet processing cannot begin until association is complete. During normal operation, CEs can update routes or request statistics, while FEs can report events such as a port failure.
sections.plainLanguage: First, managers choose which control and forwarding elements belong together. The elements then authenticate, exchange capability information, and finish setup before packet processing begins.

sections.title: Restarts and Security
sections.content:
If a CE restarts and graceful restart is supported, its FEs can retain forwarding state for a limited time. A timer set by the CE eventually expires that cached state. If an FE leaves or fails, the CE informs routing protocols and may update the forwarding tables on remaining FEs.

The RFC identifies risks including false join requests, impersonation, replay, forged messages, eavesdropping, and denial of service through an external interface. It calls for authentication and integrity protection where needed and requires rate limiting at both CEs and FEs to limit message floods.
sections.plainLanguage: Forwarding elements may keep their existing state briefly during a supported control-element restart. The communication link also needs protection against false messages and traffic floods.
